column4: The section treats the two eyes as a gift and a witness; here ears, eyes, and skins testify against their owners, turning the organs into evidence.
The section connects the spoken claim in 90:6 with a watching presence; this ayah says no word is uttered without a ready recorder, using the source-section root ر ق ب in رَقِيبٌ عَتِيدٌ.
The source image joins a watching eye to what is hidden; this ayah names both “خَائِنَةَ الْأَعْيُنِ” and what breasts conceal, including a furtive glance and inward secrecy.
After naming the destroyed peoples, this ayah says the Lord is “بِالْمِرْصَادِ,” at a watchful post; it makes the section's lookout image a statement about divine oversight.

The section says the creator of eyes knows seeing; here the Creator says He knows the soul's whispered thoughts and is nearer than the jugular vein, extending oversight beyond what an eye can observe.
Against the assumption that no one saw the person, the ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it: “يَرَهُ.” The deed returns to its doer as visible consequence.
The next ayah completes 99:7 by saying an atom's weight of evil will also be seen; the section's point about no deed being unwitnessed thus includes the reverse moral case.
The section's root ر ق ب includes a guardian; this ayah says guardians are assigned over people, making the unseen watcher an explicit Qur'anic scene.
Linked to 82:10, this ayah identifies the guardians as noble recording scribes; it explains what their watching does.
Completing 82:10–11, this ayah says the scribes know what people do, specifying the conduct their record covers.
Even a private conversation among three has Allah as the fourth, and He informs them of their deeds on the Day of Resurrection; the ayah makes secrecy no shelter from the watcher.
The section recalls that eyes were given to a person; this ayah says hearing, sight, and heart will each be questioned, making the gifts answerable for their use.
The section's dictionary branch for ع ي ن describes keeping someone “under my eye”; Allah tells Moses he was made to grow “عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي,” an eye of care and protection.
Noah is told to make the ship under Allah's eyes and revelation; this is the section's protective-eye sense applied to a watched act.
The ship is built under Allah's eyes and revelation, repeating the section's ع ي ن sense of watching over and safeguarding someone or something.
Noah's ark sails under Allah's eyes; the section's protective-eye meaning is pictured as oversight of the vessel through the flood.
The Prophet is told to be patient under Allah's eyes; this directly echoes the section's dictionary phrase for someone kept and watched over.
The ayah stages game within reach of hands and spears, then says the test is who fears Allah unseen; it joins the section's hidden hunter/prey sense to the question of conduct when people cannot see.
The ayah says Allah is “رَقِيبًا” over people in its command to heed Him and kinship; that is the source-section root ر ق ب in its guardian/watchful sense.
Jesus says Allah was “الرَّقِيبَ عَلَيْهِمْ,” watchful over his people; the source-section root ر ق ب names this very guarding stance.
Allah says He brought people into being and gave them hearing, sight, and hearts; this directly answers the section's question about who made the eyes and what their gift implies.
People emerge knowing nothing, then Allah gives them hearing, sight, and hearts; the verse presents sight as a created gift that makes the section's question about its giver pointed.
Allah says He made hearing, sight, and hearts for people, yet few give thanks; it repeats the created-senses detail and links it to accountability for a gift.
After forming the human and breathing life into him, Allah makes hearing, sight, and hearts; this is another direct account of the eye as something bestowed by its Maker.
The human is created and tested, then made hearing and seeing; this connects the section's created eyes to the moral testing of what a person does while seen.
The section explicitly recalls the one whose scales are light; this ayah supplies that condition, which leads into the question and fire in 101:10–11.
The section quotes “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا هِيَهْ” as an example of the source-section root د ر ي opening a question about the unknown; this is that exact question.
The answer is “نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ”; it completes the question at 101:10 and makes explicit the fire the section says this formula often reveals.
The section describes a person gathering and counting wealth; this ayah says he amassed wealth and counted it, the behavior that frames the question in 104:5.
The section quotes “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا الْحُطَمَةُ” as another use of its د ر ي question formula, here following the wealth-counter.
The answer is the kindled fire of Allah; it completes 104:5 and exemplifies the fire-answer the section draws out from this formula.
The person given his book in his left hand says he did not know what his account was; this is the section's exact د ر ي example of knowledge turned back on the speaker.
The righteous spend wealth on relatives, orphans, needy people, and those in bondage; this joins the section's orphan/poor feeding and neck release within one account of righteousness.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive; this brings together the section's feeding of the hungry and its release of a neck, with mercy extended even to a captive.
The ayah describes shackles placed on the disbelievers' necks; this reverses the section's freeing of a neck, and its next ayah adds that their sight is blocked.
Allah's statement that He is with people wherever they are and sees what they do restates the section's claim that an unseen act remains in view.
The section's watcher/guardian senses are made universal here: every soul has a protector over it, even though this ayah uses حَافِظ rather than the source-section root.
The section's dictionary describes a lookout and a hunter's hiding place; this ayah orders the pursuers to lie in wait at every ambush, a concrete scene of concealed watching in a different setting.
During the prayer in danger, groups take turns praying while carrying weapons and remaining alert; this gives the section's guardian sense a concrete human scene of watchfulness.

The jinn describe sitting at stations to gather news by listening; this parallels the source-section's dictionary sense of عَيْن as a scout sent to collect news, though the Qur'anic scouts listen rather than look.
The ayah asks who could restore hearing and sight if Allah took them away; it marks the eyes as a revocable gift rather than a power a person owns.
The section's “insān of the eye” is a small image of the person seen within another's pupil; here a person is described as a witness against himself, turning the self into its own evidence.
Allah promises to show signs in the horizons and within people until the truth is clear; this gives the section's dictionary link between ayat and visible signs a direct Qur'anic counterpart.
People on the heights recognize others by their marks; the visible mark identifies a person, a concrete parallel to the section's lexicon calling a person's recognizable form an “āya.”
Criminals are recognized by their marks and seized; the section's dictionary sense of a person's visible form as an āya is echoed by the body serving as an identifying sign.
The Prophet is told he would recognize the hypocrites by their marks and speech; visible appearance functions as a sign of the person, parallel to the source-section's secondary āya sense.
Moses reports “إِنِّي آنَسْتُ نَارًا,” using the source-section root ء ن س for perceiving something by sight; the scene supplies a literal instance of that dictionary sense.
Moses again says “آنَسْتُ نَارًا”; this repeats the section's dictionary use of the root ء ن س for seeing or perceiving, here in a fire-seen scene.
In the third telling Moses says “آنَسْتُ نَارًا”; it repeats the source-section root's sense of seeing something, with the fire as the noticed object.
The opening rebuke concerns turning away when the blind man came; linked to 80:2, it makes the section's physical eye and the limits of sight relevant to who seeks guidance.
The visitor is described as blind; this gives the section's contrast between the eye and blindness a human scene in which lack of sight does not remove the need to be heard.
The next ayah asks what could make the Prophet know whether the man might purify himself; its د ر ي wording echoes the section's question about what human beings can know and what is disclosed.
The ayah says his destination is “هَاوِيَةٌ”; linked to 101:10–11, it begins the answer to what awaits the person with light scales.
The next ayah says the fire rises over hearts; it completes the fire scene after 104:6, showing the punishment reaches inward as well as burning visibly.
This is another “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ” question, this time about Saqar; the section specifically says the formula often opens onto fire.
Saqar neither leaves nor spares; linked to 74:27, this supplies the fire's consequence after the question.
The next ayah says Saqar scorches people; it completes the fire description following 74:27 and 74:28.
The question “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا الْحَاقَّةُ” repeats the source-section's formula for something whose reality the hearer cannot supply unaided.
“وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا يَوْمُ الْفَصْلِ” uses the same source-section question formula about the Day of Decision, a reality the question makes the hearer await.
The next ayah warns of woe to deniers on that day; it completes the question at 77:14 with its consequence for those who reject it.
This ayah asks “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ,” repeating the source-section's question-formula about what cannot be grasped without disclosure.
It repeats the question about the Day of Judgment; the repetition completes the doubled question started in 82:17.
The answer says no soul can help another and command that day belongs to Allah; it completes 82:17–18 by stating the boundary of human power.
The same “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ” form asks what Sijjin is; as in the section, a question marks knowledge that must be supplied rather than presumed.
Sijjin is identified as a written record; it completes the question in 83:8 with an image of deeds fixed in a record, consonant with the section's unseen watcher.
This ayah repeats the question-formula for Illiyyun, extending the section's examples beyond questions answered by fire.
Illiyyun is identified as a written record; it completes 83:19 by making the unknown a record of deeds.
The next ayah says those brought near witness that record; it completes the image in 83:20 with observers, meeting the section's watcher theme.
The question “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا الطَّارِقُ” repeats the source-section's formula and points to a visible night-comer in the next ayah.
The answer is “النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ,” a piercing star; it completes 86:2 with a visible sign in the night sky.
The ayah asks “وَمَا أَدْرَاكَ مَا لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ,” repeating the source-section's question about something the hearer cannot know unaided.
The next ayah says the Night of Decree is better than a thousand months; it completes the unknown named in 97:2 with its revealed measure.

After naming the revealed Book and balance, the ayah asks what could make the hearer know that the Hour may be near; it repeats the source-section root د ر ي around knowledge not controlled by people.
The question “وَمَا يُدْرِيكَ” asks what could make the Prophet know, then says the Hour may be near; this echoes the section's root for what is disclosed about an unknown reality.
The Prophet says he had not known the Book or faith before revelation; the source-section root د ر ي likewise marks the human limit that God's disclosure can cross.
The ayah makes freeing a believing slave part of expiation; this parallels the section's فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ and uses the neck/manumission image in a legal setting.
One expiation option is freeing a slave, alongside feeding needy people; it closely joins the section's release of a neck with its feeding of the hungry.
A share of alms is assigned “فِي الرِّقَابِ,” for freeing people from bondage; this directly parallels the section's release of a neck.
A man who makes the forbidden comparison about his wife must free a slave before returning to her; this repeats the section's act of freeing a neck in a different legal context.
If he cannot free a slave, he must fast, then feed sixty poor people if unable; the neighbor ayah completes 58:3 and explicitly moves from manumission to feeding.
Slaves seeking a contract of freedom are to be given one, and helped from God's wealth; it gives another concrete Qur'anic route from bondage toward release.
After battle, captives may be released by grace or ransom; it is a parallel act of releasing bound people, though the context is prisoners of war rather than a slave's neck.
Asked what to spend, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, and needy people; this matches the section's close orphan and destitute recipients as concrete recipients of giving.
A recognized share of wealth belongs to the petitioner and deprived; this makes the section's feeding of the hungry a matter of others' due, not merely private generosity.
A barrier before and behind them leaves them unable to see; linked to 36:8, it joins bound necks to blocked vision, meeting two elements of the section's image.
The section asks whether anyone saw the man; this rebuke asks whether the one obstructing prayer knows that Allah sees him, making the denied observer explicit.
The section's imagined privacy is stated almost exactly in the condemned people's thought that Allah did not know much of what they did; the verse names the false premise behind acting unseen.
People may hide their speech and plans from other people, but the ayah says they cannot hide them from Allah, who is present with them in the night counsel; it directly overturns presumed privacy.
The people ask whether God hears their secret counsel, and the answer says the messengers are present recording it; hidden speech in the section's image is likewise not unwitnessed.
The man thought he would never return, but the ayah says his Lord had always seen him; this reverses the section's imagined freedom from observation.
The ayah condemns concealing clear proofs and guidance after they were made clear; it fits the section's reading of sign-deniers as people who cover what ought to be seen.
The People of the Book were charged to make scripture clear and not conceal it, but cast it away; this parallels the section's contrast between visible signs and their denial or covering.
The ayah says the covering is removed and sight becomes sharp, “فَبَصَرُكَ الْيَوْمَ حَدِيدٌ”; it reverses the section's man's imagined control of what can be seen by making the hidden clear.
The ayah sets a boundary on sight: eyes do not comprehend Allah, while He comprehends all eyes; the section's eye-gift therefore does not make human vision unlimited.
These people have eyes but do not see with them; this is the section's sharp reversal of the given two eyes as a faculty of perception.
Thamud were shown guidance but preferred blindness to it; the ayah makes sight's moral refusal explicit, beyond the physical eye described in the section.
Allah says He could wipe out their eyes, after which they would rush toward the path but not see; this reverses the eye as a dependable gift and joins sight to guidance.
The ayah describes eyes covered from Allah's reminder and inability to hear it; it shows how an eye can be present yet barred from the signs it should perceive.
After describing a person who makes desire his god, the ayah says Allah seals hearing and heart and places a covering over sight; it reverses the eyes' gift into impaired perception.
Past peoples were given hearing, sight, and hearts, but these availed them nothing when they denied the signs; the senses in the section can be received yet refused as instruments of recognition.
This ayah condemns failing to honor the orphan; linked to 89:18, it begins the opposite of the section's care for the orphan and poor.
The people do not urge one another to feed the poor; this reverses the section's feeding on a day of hunger and shows communal neglect.
People in Saqar say they were not among those who fed the poor; this directly contrasts the section's feeding of the hungry with a deed associated with punishment.
The condemned person did not believe in Allah; linked to 69:34, this pairs disbelief with the failure to feed the poor, against the section's joined faith and mercy.
The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor; this is the direct negative counterpart to the section's hungry-day feeding.
The surah opens by asking who denies the Judgment; linked to 107:2–3, this introduces denial joined to neglect of the orphan and poor, a reversal of the section's faith and mercy.
The denier repels the orphan; linked to 107:3, it adds the orphan to the neglected poor and reverses the section's mercy toward both.
The denier does not urge feeding the poor; this is a direct negation of the section's act of feeding the hungry.
The condemned man is seized and shackled; this is the reversal of the section's “فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ,” a freed neck turned into punishment by restraint.
He is then cast into the Blaze; linked to 69:30 and 69:32, this completes the restrained man's punishment in the same left-hand-book scene that the section invokes at 69:26.
A chain of seventy cubits is placed around him; linked to 69:30, it intensifies the opposite of the section's freed neck.
The disbelievers are prepared chains, shackles, and fire; this is the bodily opposite of the section's release of a neck and its contrast between the two final groups.
The ayah says shackles will be put around the disbelievers' necks; it turns the section's freed neck into a sign of judgment's restraint.
Wrongdoers are seen bound together in chains on the day of Judgment; this reverses the release of a neck in the section and makes the bound state visible.
The people of Hell are described with shackles and chains around their necks; this is a direct bodily reversal of the section's emancipation image.
They are dragged into boiling water and then the Fire; linked to 40:71, it completes the scene of those bound by the neck.
The ayah names chains and a blazing fire prepared for the guilty; this is a contrary fate to the section's freeing of a neck.
It adds food that chokes and painful punishment; linked to 73:12, it extends the punishment scene opposite the section's feeding of the hungry.
The ayah says no action or state is absent from Allah, down to an atom's weight, and that it is recorded; this extends the section's unseen-observer claim to every deed and its record.
People fold their breasts and cover themselves to hide from God, yet He knows what they conceal and reveal; this directly stages the hiddenness the section's man presumes.
The ayah equates one who hides a statement with one who declares it, and the person hidden by night with the one abroad by day; it directly dissolves the public/private boundary in the section.
People are told to act because Allah, His Messenger, and the believers will see their deeds; this makes the section's unseen action explicitly visible and answerable.
The command to “watch for” the coming day uses ارتقب from the source-section root ر ق ب, in the section's sense of watching and awaiting what is coming.
Allah does not disclose His unseen to أَحَدًا, “anyone”; this meets the section's link between أَحَدٌ (“anyone”) and عين (“eye”) in a verse about who may know what is hidden.
The next ayah makes an exception for a chosen messenger and places guards before and behind him; it completes 72:26 with both disclosure and watchfulness.
Each person's deed is fastened to his neck, then brought out as an open record; this joins the section's neck and watcher details in one bodily image of unavoidable accounting.
The person is told to read his book and finds himself sufficient as his own accountant; it completes 17:13 by showing what the neck-borne record requires.
The opened book omits neither small nor great deeds, and people see what they did present before them; this gives the section's claim of unwitnessed acts an exhaustive record scene.
On the Day of Judgment, people's tongues, hands, and feet testify to what they did; this repeats the section's image of bodily faculties becoming witnesses against their owner.
The mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what people earned; it repeats the bodily testimony scene with a different set of organs.
The ayah says a person's striving will be seen, سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ; it directly joins the section's sight motif to deeds and their recompense.
Every soul comes with a driver and a witness, سَائِقٌ وَشَهِيدٌ; this makes the section's unseen watcher an explicit companion at judgment.
A person with abundant provision says his Lord has honored him; this parallels the section's wealthy man's assumption that material spending proves his security.
The ayah says people love wealth intensely; this sharpens the parallel to the man who boasts of spending heaps of money while leaving the needy uncared for.

The passage describes the person who considers himself self-sufficient, وَأَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَىٰ; this is a close parallel to the section's wealthy man who imagines himself beyond anyone's power or sight.

The following scene turns to a blind man who comes seeking guidance; unlike the affluent self-satisfied person, he is the one asking for attention, paralleling the section's care for the poor and its limits of sight.
The needy who refrain from asking are recognized by their mark, بِسِيمَاهُمْ; this meets the section's image of a person as a visible sign and its mention of the destitute covered in dust.
The wealth-counter thinks his wealth will make him last forever; this exposes the self-security behind the counting that the section connects to the question and fire.

Clear proofs have come, and whoever sees benefits himself while whoever is blind harms himself; the verse joins visible signs, moral blindness, and the limit of a guardian, all developed in the section.
The ayah says Allah encompasses what the messengers have and counts everything; it completes 72:26–27 by confirming the disclosure and the full accounting around it.
This ayah identifies the speaker in 69:26 as the one given his book in his left hand; it is the needed context for the section's quotation of his words.
The speaker says he will cast the man into Saqar; it frames the “what is Saqar?” question in 74:27 that the section cites as a fire-opening formula.
The ayah says the wealth-counter will be thrown into the Crusher; it introduces the question at 104:5 and its fire-answer in 104:6.
Nothing in earth or heaven is hidden from Allah; this supplies a concise boundary to the man's belief that no one saw him.
Allah knows every leaf that falls and every grain, wet or dry, recorded in a clear book; this gives the section's unseen-observer claim a concrete image of nothing escaping notice.
Whether people conceal or declare their speech, Allah knows what is within their breasts; it directly joins hidden words to inward knowledge.
What people disclose or conceal within themselves is still brought to account by Allah; it makes inner hiddenness answerable, as in the section's image.
Linked to 13:10, successive guardians preserve each person by Allah's command; it supplies the watcher behind the ayah's contrast of hidden and public conduct.
The ayah closes with Allah as رَقِيبًا over all things, repeating the source-section root ر ق ب in its watchful-guardian sense.
The awaited smoke covers people and is a painful torment; it completes 44:10 by showing what the root ر ق ب commands the hearer to watch for.
The closing command “watch; they too are watching” repeats the source-section root ر ق ب as waiting for an outcome.
The command وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا forbids spying on one another; it gives the section's secondary image of an eye sent to gather news a human setting and a moral boundary.

The example contrasts an owned slave unable to act with a person given good provision who spends openly and secretly; it joins the section's freed neck, hidden conduct, and boast about wealth in one comparison.
The self remains witness even if it offers excuses; it completes 75:14 by showing that self-testimony cannot be evaded.
The next ayah says Allah will pay them their true recompense; it completes 24:24 by linking bodily testimony to judgment.
The day when hidden matters are exposed, تَبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ, gives a direct counterpart to the section's insistence that what seems unseen will become known.
Allah teaches the human what he did not know; this gives the section's point about what cannot be known without disclosure a concrete parallel.
The addressee attends to the self-sufficient man; it completes 80:5 and sharpens the contrast with the blind seeker who follows.
The blind visitor comes with concern and fear; it completes 80:8 by showing his earnest stance, which makes the turning-away in 80:10 consequential.
The addressee is distracted from the blind seeker; it completes the scene begun in 80:8 and contrasts with the section's call to feed and aid those in need.
The believers' mark is visible on their faces; this is a bodily identifier parallel to the section's secondary āya sense of a person's visible form.
The written records are spread open; this is a specific afterlife scene of deeds becoming visible, fitting the section's account of unwitnessed acts.
Whether people disclose what is within themselves or conceal it, Allah knows it; this is another direct boundary on the privacy imagined in the section.

Those who deny the signs are gradually drawn on from where they do not know; this parallels the section's secondary d-r-y image of a hunter approaching prey unseen, though the verse itself describes divine enticement rather than hunting.
The next ayah says the deniers are given respite and that God's plan is firm; it completes the gradual, unperceived approach in 7:182.
Those who deny the Reminder are gradually drawn on from where they do not know; this repeats the specific unseen-approach image in 7:182 and the section's hunter/prey lexical image.
The next ayah grants them respite; it completes the unseen gradual drawing in 68:44.
People are brought forward with no hidden thing of theirs concealed; this states the opposite of the left-hand man's imagined privacy and leads into the book scenes.
The person given his book in his right hand says to read it; this supplies the opposite book-receiving outcome to 69:25–26, which the section cites.
He says he knew he would meet his account; it completes 69:19 and contrasts with the left-hand speaker's not knowing his account in 69:26.
The record speaks truth and states that what people did was being written; this repeats the section's image of actions made present as testimony.
The person interprets reduced provision as humiliation; the surah immediately corrects that judgment by pointing to neglect of the orphan and poor, reversing wealth as a measure of worth.
The condemned are asked what brought them into Saqar; it introduces the punishment whose answer in 74:44 includes failure to feed the poor.
The orphan is not to be oppressed; this reverses the neglect of vulnerable people that the section contrasts with mercy.
The person who asks is not to be repelled; this reverses the section's call to feed and aid the needy.
Every soul is held in pledge for what it earned; this is a boundary opposite to the section's freeing of a neck.
The next ayah excepts the people of the right; it completes 74:38 with the divided outcome echoed by the section's companions of the right and left.
Heavy scales bring a good life, the explicit reverse of the light scales and fire the section names.
The pleasant life completes the heavy-scale side of the contrast with the light-scaled person in 101:8–11.
The ayah says it is not the eyes that are blind but the hearts in the breasts; this sets a boundary between the section's sensory eye and inward recognition.
The blind and seeing are not equal, nor are believers who do good and the evildoer; this explicitly joins perception with the moral distinction made in the section.
The disbelievers' hearing is sealed and a covering is over their sight; this repeats the section's contrast between eyes given and eyes unable or unwilling to perceive.
The ayah asks whether the blind and the seeing, or darkness and light, are equal; it uses sight as a measure of recognition, directly matching the section's eye-and-guidance link.
The ayah asks whether the blind and the seeing are equal; this is another direct Qur'anic formulation of the perception boundary developed in the section.
The blind and the seeing are declared unequal; this repeats the section's physical and moral sight contrast in a brief direct formulation.
Some look toward the Prophet, but he cannot guide the blind who do not see; the verse distinguishes looking from true perception as the section does.
